questions.q: According to the summary, what pushed home-cooked meals aside in the 1950s?
a: More women working, television, and clever marketing
Rising food prices and a shortage of ingredients
Government restrictions on home kitchens
A sharp decline in the number of schools
questions.why: Lesson 1 links the change to careers outside the home, the new appeal of TV and heavy advertising of convenience food.

questions.q: Why does the summary say we eat far more fat than we should?
a: We have no taste buds for fat, so we cannot sense how much we have had
Fat contains fewer calories than sugar does
Our bodies naturally stop craving fat after a while
Food labels overstate the fat content of products
questions.why: Lesson 2 explains that we can taste salt and sugar but not fat, so more always seems better.

questions.q: How much more fat do Americans eat daily than they should, per the summary?
a: About 50 percent more
About 10 percent more
About 25 percent more
About 90 percent more
questions.why: Lesson 2 states that Americans average 50 percent more fat every day than they should.

questions.q: Why do processed food companies value fat so highly?
a: It improves texture and extends shelf life
It is cheaper to produce than water
It removes the need for salt and sugar
It makes nutrition labels easier to write
questions.why: Lesson 2 notes that fat adds appealing texture and keeps products sellable for longer.

questions.q: What happened when Campbell cut sodium from its soups?
a: Customers complained about the taste and sales fell
Sales rose sharply and rivals copied the change
The government praised the company publicly
The low-salt soups became its best sellers
questions.why: Lesson 3 says shoppers found the soups bland, sales dropped, and the sodium content went back up.
